overview.what_it_is: A mixed review of number, fractions, ratio, measures, money, shapes, and angles.

format_facts.label: Lesson type
format_facts.value: Mixed review across earlier Year 5 topics

format_facts.label: Main skills
format_facts.value: Number, measures, fractions, ratio, money, and geometry

format_facts.label: Answer style
format_facts.value: Show each step, then write a clear sentence

format_facts.label: Useful tools
format_facts.value: Ruler, protractor, pencil, and squared paper

scoring_factors.name: Correct method
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the right maths rule was chosen.

scoring_factors.name: Correct working
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether each step follows from the last.

scoring_factors.name: Correct units
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether answers use dollars, metres, or square units.

scoring_factors.name: Clear answer
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the final sentence answers the question.

scoring_factors.name: Reasonable check
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the answer fits the size of the problem.

critical_rules: Read the question twice before choosing a method.
Change measurements into the same unit before comparing.
For a fraction of an amount, multiply by the top number.
For a ratio, find the value of one part first.
Area uses square units. Perimeter uses ordinary length units.
Angles on a straight line total $180^\circ$.
Write every final answer with its correct unit.

learning_goals: You will subtract thousands from larger whole numbers.
You will round whole numbers to the nearest thousand.
You will multiply and divide by $10$, $100$, and $1{,}000$.
You will change litres, millilitres, metres, centimetres, and time.
You will write parts of amounts as fractions.
You will solve money problems with several steps.
You will use fractions to find used and leftover amounts.
You will share amounts using two-part and three-part ratios.
You will find area, perimeter, and missing angles.

core_method.name: Read → Sort → Plan → Work → Label → Check
core_method.summary: First find the topic. Then choose one clear method.

steps.detail: Read every word and circle the needed answer.
Name the topic: number, fraction, ratio, measure, or shape.
Write the rule or bar model before calculating.
Show one small step on each line.
Add the correct unit to the answer.
Estimate or use the inverse operation.

core_method.formula: READ + CHOOSE THE TOPIC + SHOW STEPS + CHECK

techniques.name: Use place value for powers of ten
techniques.purpose: Multiply or divide without long working.
how_to: Find how many zeros are in the power of ten.
Move each digit left when multiplying.
Move each digit right when dividing.
Check that the answer grows or becomes smaller.
techniques.example: $58{,}000 \div 100 = 580$ because digits move two places right.
techniques.why_it_matters: Place value explains the change, not a zero trick.
techniques.common_error: Removing zeros without checking the place values.

techniques.name: Round with the halfway digit
how_to: Find the thousands digit.
Look at the hundreds digit beside it.
Round up when that digit is $5$ or more.
Round down when that digit is $4$ or less.
techniques.why_it_matters: Rounding gives a useful estimate before exact work.
techniques.common_error: Looking at the tens digit instead of hundreds.

techniques.name: Make units match first
techniques.purpose: Compare or form fractions from measurements.
how_to: Choose the smaller unit for both amounts.
Use $1\text{ L} = 1{,}000\text{ mL}$.
Use $1\text{ m} = 100\text{ cm}$.
Then form the fraction or complete the operation.
techniques.why_it_matters: A fraction only compares amounts in matching units.

techniques.name: Draw a bar model for fraction problems
techniques.purpose: Show the whole, used part, and leftover part.
how_to: Draw one bar for the whole amount.
Split it into equal parts from the bottom number.
Mark the used parts from the top number.
Count the unmarked parts for what remains.
techniques.example: For $\frac{5}{8}$ used, mark $5$ of $8$ parts. Then $3$ parts remain.
techniques.why_it_matters: The picture stops used and leftover parts being mixed.
techniques.common_error: Finding the used amount when the question asks what remains.

techniques.name: Find one ratio part
techniques.purpose: Share or scale an amount fairly.
how_to: Add all ratio numbers.
Divide the total amount by that sum.
Multiply one part by each ratio number.
Check that all shares add to the total.
techniques.why_it_matters: One part links the ratio to the real amount.
techniques.common_error: Dividing the total by only one ratio number.

techniques.name: Split composite shapes
techniques.purpose: Find area and perimeter of joined rectangles.
how_to: Split the shape into simple rectangles.
Find each rectangle area.
Add areas without counting overlap twice.
Trace only the outside edges for perimeter.
techniques.why_it_matters: Small rectangles are easier than one odd shape.
techniques.common_error: Adding an inside edge to the perimeter.

techniques.name: Use angle totals
techniques.purpose: Find an unknown angle without measuring.
how_to: Name the angle rule shown.
Write the full angle total.
Add the known angles.
Subtract that sum from the full total.
techniques.why_it_matters: The rule gives an exact answer.
techniques.common_error: Using $360^\circ$ for angles on a straight line.

worked_examples.title: Round and use place value
worked_examples.input: Round $42{,}680$ to the nearest thousand. Then work out $728 \times 100$.
worked_examples.decoding: The first part uses rounding. The second uses place value.
worked_examples.plan: Check the hundreds digit. Then move digits two places left.
worked_examples.model_answer: For rounding, the thousands digit is $2$. The hundreds digit is $6$. Since $6 \ge 5$, round up. So $42{,}680 \approx 43{,}000$. For multiplication, each digit moves two places left. Thus $728 \times 100 = 72{,}800$. The answers are $43{,}000$ and $72{,}800$.

annotations.comment: This tells us to round the thousands up.
The sign shows an estimate, not an exact equality.
Multiplying by $100$ changes each place value.
The answer is one hundred times larger.

worked_examples.title: Find a fraction of a measurement
worked_examples.input: What fraction of $3\text{ L}$ is $800\text{ mL}$?
worked_examples.decoding: Both amounts must use the same unit first.
worked_examples.plan: Change litres to millilitres. Form the fraction. Make it simplest.
worked_examples.model_answer: $3\text{ L} = 3 \times 1{,}000\text{ mL} = 3{,}000\text{ mL}$. The fraction is $\frac{800}{3{,}000}$. Divide the top and bottom by $200$: $\frac{800 \div 200}{3{,}000 \div 200} = \frac{4}{15}$. Therefore, $800\text{ mL}$ is $\frac{4}{15}$ of $3\text{ L}$.

annotations.comment: The units now match.
The part goes on top. The whole goes below.
Both numbers are divided by the same value.
This fraction is in simplest form.

worked_examples.title: Find money left from a fraction
worked_examples.input: Lauren spent $\frac{3}{5}$ of her money on a refrigerator costing $756$. How much money remained?
worked_examples.decoding: The price is $3$ equal parts. The whole amount is $5$ parts.
worked_examples.plan: Bar model: draw $5$ equal parts. Mark $3$ parts as $756$. Find one part, then find $2$ parts left.
worked_examples.model_answer: Bar model: $5$ equal parts show all her money. The refrigerator uses $3$ parts. First find one part: $756 \div 3 = 252$. The money left is $2$ parts: $252 \times 2 = 504$. Check the whole: $252 \times 5 = 1{,}260$. Also, $1{,}260 - 756 = 504$. Lauren had $504$ dollars left.

annotations.comment: This finds the value of one equal part.
Two of the five parts were not spent.
This rebuilds the whole amount.
Subtraction checks the result.

worked_examples.title: Use ratio for a rectangular field
worked_examples.input: A field has length-to-width ratio $4:3$. Its length is $20\text{ m}$. Find its area and perimeter.
worked_examples.decoding: The length is $4$ parts. The width is $3$ parts.
worked_examples.plan: Bar model: draw $4$ parts for length and $3$ for width. Find one part. Then find width, area, and perimeter.
worked_examples.model_answer: Bar model: the $20\text{ m}$ length has $4$ equal parts. One part is $20 \div 4 = 5\text{ m}$. The width is $3 \times 5\text{ m} = 15\text{ m}$. Area: $20\text{ m} \times 15\text{ m} = 300\text{ m}^2$. Perimeter: $2 \times (20\text{ m} + 15\text{ m}) = 2 \times 35\text{ m} = 70\text{ m}$. The field has area $300\text{ m}^2$ and perimeter $70\text{ m}$.

annotations.comment: This finds one ratio part.
The width has three equal parts.
Area uses square metres.
Perimeter uses metres, not square metres.

worked_examples.title: Find area from a triangle perimeter
worked_examples.input: A right triangle has perimeter $36\text{ m}$, height $9\text{ m}$, and longest side $15\text{ m}$. Find its area.
worked_examples.decoding: Use the perimeter to find the missing base first.
worked_examples.plan: Subtract the two known sides from the perimeter. Then use half base times height.
worked_examples.model_answer: The missing base is $36\text{ m} - 9\text{ m} - 15\text{ m} = 12\text{ m}$. The triangle area is $\frac{1}{2} \times 12\text{ m} \times 9\text{ m} = 6\text{ m} \times 9\text{ m} = 54\text{ m}^2$. The area of the triangle is $54\text{ m}^2$.

annotations.comment: This is the total of all three sides.
This is the missing base.
A triangle is half a matching rectangle.
Area needs square units.

worked_examples.title: Find a missing angle
worked_examples.input: Two angles lie on a straight line. One angle is $127^\circ$. Find the other angle, $x$.
worked_examples.decoding: Angles on a straight line add to $180^\circ$.
worked_examples.model_answer: Angles on a straight line total $180^\circ$. So $x + 127^\circ = 180^\circ$. Therefore, $x = 180^\circ - 127^\circ = 53^\circ$. The missing angle is $53^\circ$.

annotations.comment: This is the full straight-line angle.
The two neighbouring angles make the line.
Subtract to find the missing part.
The answer includes the degree sign.

worked_examples.title: Correct a leftover-fraction mistake
worked_examples.input: Lynn had $8\text{ m}$ of string. She used $\frac{5}{8}$. A pupil answered $5\text{ m}$ left. Correct the mistake.
worked_examples.decoding: The fraction given is the used part, not the leftover part.
worked_examples.plan: Bar model: split the whole into $8$ parts. Mark $5$ used. Count the $3$ parts left.
worked_examples.model_answer: Bar model: $8$ equal parts show the whole string. Lynn used $5$ parts, so $8 - 5 = 3$ parts remain. The leftover fraction is $1 - \frac{5}{8} = \frac{3}{8}$. Now find $\frac{3}{8}$ of $8\text{ m}$: $8\text{ m} \times \frac{3}{8} = 3\text{ m}$. The pupil found the used amount. Lynn had $3\text{ m}$ left.

annotations.comment: This is the used fraction.
This is the fraction that remains.
The fraction is applied to the whole length.
This answers what was left.

items.when_to_use: Use it when digits move after multiplying or dividing.
Use it when rounding to a whole thousand.
Use it for a close answer before exact work.
Use the opposite operation to check an answer.
Use it for the answer to multiplication.
Use it for the answer to division.
Use it for what is left after division.
Use it for the answer to subtraction.
It shows how many equal parts are chosen.
It shows how many equal parts make the whole.
Multiply the whole by the given fraction.
Use it when no common factor remains.
Use it to compare equal-sized parts.
Find this before working out each share.
Use it for one person's part of a total.
Add all parts or amounts.
Use it when changing one measure unit to another.
Use it for a small amount of liquid.
Use it for a short length.
Use it for area answers.
Use it for space inside a shape.
Use it for distance around a shape.
Use it for an angle of $90^\circ$.
Use it when neighbouring angles total $180^\circ$.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: It may change the answer by a whole thousand.
common_mistakes.fix: For nearest thousand, check the hundreds digit.

common_mistakes.mistake: Adding zeros without thinking about place value.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: This fails when a number ends with zeros.
common_mistakes.fix: Move each digit by the needed number of places.
Change both amounts into the same unit first.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the given fraction as the leftover fraction.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The question may give the used part instead.
common_mistakes.fix: Find the missing fraction with $1 - \text{used fraction}$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dividing a ratio total by one ratio number.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The total belongs to all ratio parts.
common_mistakes.fix: Add every ratio number before dividing.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Perimeter is a length, not an area.
common_mistakes.fix: Use metres or centimetres for perimeter.

common_mistakes.mistake: Counting inside edges in a composite perimeter.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Only outside edges form the boundary.
common_mistakes.fix: Trace the outside with a finger before adding.

common_mistakes.mistake: Measuring an angle when an exact rule is given.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: A drawing may not be to scale.

time_budget.focus: Bar models, money, and leftover amounts
One-part method, area, perimeter, and angles
Find errors and explain each fix

drills.name: Round and check
drills.instructions: Round $10$ numbers to the nearest thousand. Mark the hundreds digit each time.

drills.name: Unit match cards
drills.instructions: Match $8$ litre, millilitre, metre, centimetre, hour, and minute pairs.

drills.name: Fraction bar models
drills.instructions: Draw $6$ bars showing a used fraction and the part left.

drills.name: Ratio one-part drill
drills.instructions: Solve $6$ sharing problems. Write the value of one part first.

drills.name: Shape trace
drills.instructions: Trace $5$ composite shapes. Mark outside edges before finding perimeter.

practice_plan.routine: Work for $20$ minutes. Check for $5$ minutes. Correct every mistake in a new line.

mastery_checklist: I can subtract $1{,}000$ from a larger number.
I can round a number to the nearest thousand.
I can multiply and divide by $10$, $100$, and $1{,}000$.
I can change litres and millilitres.
I can change metres and centimetres.
I can change hours and minutes.
I can find and reduce a fraction of a whole.
I can solve fraction and money word problems.
I can find one ratio part and each share.
I can find area, perimeter, and missing angles.
strategy_notes: Start with questions you can identify quickly.
Underline words like left, altogether, more, and each.
Write units beside numbers during the working.
Estimate money and whole-number answers before exact work.
Draw a bar model when several amounts are linked.
For ratio, write the total number of parts first.
For diagrams, mark known lengths and angle totals.
Use the textbook diagram for questions needing measured lengths or angles.
